The engine hummed a low, steady song as Mr. Abernathy steered the charter bus toward Oakhaven. Twenty-three souls, mostly middle-aged and radiating a shared enthusiasm, bounced gently in their seats. They were headed to the annual Ironwood Hawks versus the Riverbend Raptors lumberjack competition, a regional spectacle of axe throwing, log rolling, and beard-growing. Mr. Abernathy had driven countless groups to countless events, but the energy on this particular bus was… palpable. He adjusted his rearview mirror, a slight smile playing on his lips.

The halfway point arrived in the form of a sprawling rest stop, a beacon of fluorescent lights and the aroma of fried dough. A collective sigh of relief rippled through the bus as the doors hissed open. Passengers spilled out, eager to stretch cramped limbs and raid the convenience store for sugary sustenance. Children darted between legs, teenagers huddled around phone screens, and the adults engaged in animated conversations, fueled by caffeine and the anticipation of the competition. Mr. Abernathy opted for a quiet cup of coffee and a crossword puzzle, content to observe the flurry of activity. 

Back on board, the atmosphere shifted from restless energy to fervent debate. “Hawks all the way!” declared a man sporting a particularly impressive handlebar mustache. “Raptors are the underdogs this year,” countered a woman in a Riverbend Raptors t-shirt, “and underdogs always surprise you.” Arguments flowed freely, punctuated by laughter and the rustling of snack wrappers. Mr. Abernathy listened, occasionally offering a neutral “Interesting point,” before returning to his driving. He knew better than to get drawn into the fray; his role was to transport, not to judge.

The landscape began to change, the flat farmland giving way to rolling hills dotted with towering pines. Mr. Abernathy expertly navigated a series of winding roads, his hands steady on the wheel. A sudden burst of excitement erupted from the back of the bus as the stadium came into view – a magnificent structure of wood and steel, buzzing with the energy of thousands of spectators. Finding the designated drop-off point proved to be a minor challenge, but with a careful maneuver and a strategic glance at a helpful security guard, he located the perfect spot.

He positioned the bus directly beside the grand entrance, a perfect alignment that earned a chorus of appreciative murmurs. The doors opened once more, releasing the eager crowd into the vibrant chaos of the event. Mr. Abernathy watched as they streamed towards the stadium, their faces alight with anticipation. He began his pre-departure checklist, the familiar routine a comfort in the sudden quiet.

As the last passenger disappeared into the throng, a few turned back, offering smiles and nods of gratitude. "Thanks for the ride, Mr. Abernathy!" one called out. "You got us here safe and sound!" Another simply offered a warm, heartfelt, "Much appreciated."

Mr. Abernathy returned their smiles, a quiet satisfaction settling within him. He closed the doors, the engine started with a reassuring rumble, and he turned the bus around, heading back toward home. The Ironwood Hawks and the Riverbend Raptors would have their day. He had delivered his cargo, and that was enough.



The road stretched ahead, long and familiar.
